name: Slovenian
family: Indo-European, Balto-Slavic, Slavic, South Slavic (western group)
variety: Standard Slovenian as spoken in Ljubljana. The standard accepts two accent systems: a tonemic one (pitch accent, central dialects including Ljubljana) and a non-tonemic one (stress only, used by most speakers from other regions). Both are described.
sources: Šuštaršič, Rastislav; Komar, Smiljana & Petek, Bojan (1999). Slovene. In Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, 135-139. Cambridge University Press.
Toporišič, Jože (2000). Slovenska slovnica. Maribor: Obzorja.
Srebot-Rejec, Tatjana (1988). Word Accent and Vowel Duration in Standard Slovene: An Acoustic and Linguistic Investigation. München: Otto Sagner.
Petek, Bojan; Šuštaršič, Rastislav & Komar, Smiljana (1996). An acoustic analysis of contemporary vowels of the standard Slovenian language. Proceedings of ICSLP 96, Philadelphia.
Jurgec, Peter (2011). Slovenščina ima 9 samoglasnikov. Slavistična revija 59(3).
Herrity, Peter (2000). Slovene: A Comprehensive Grammar. London: Routledge.
Priestly, T. M. S. (1993). Slovene. In B. Comrie & G. G. Corbett (eds.), The Slavonic Languages. London: Routledge.
Greenberg, Marc L. (2000). A Historical Phonology of the Slovene Language. Heidelberg: Carl Winter.
contrasts: close-mid versus open-mid vowels under stress, not shown in ordinary spelling (pot: [poːt] 'path' vs [pɔːt] 'sweat'; péti 'to sing' vs pêti 'fifth')
schwa /ə/ as a separate vowel, also stressed (pes [pəs], dež [dəʃ]), spelled e
tonemic varieties: acute versus circumflex pitch accent on long stressed syllables
traditional norm: long versus short stressed vowels, the short ones almost only in final syllables (brat [brat] vs brata [ˈbraːta])
voiced versus voiceless obstruents (neutralised word-finally and in clusters)
allophony: /ʋ/ is [ʋ] before vowels, the glide [u̯] after a vowel before a consonant or word-finally (siv [siu̯]), and [w], voiceless [ʍ] or syllabic [u] word-initially or between consonants before a consonant (vzeti [uˈzeːti], vsak [ʍsak] or [uˈsak]); the preposition v follows the same rule
written l is [u̯] at the end of a syllable in many words and in the masculine past participle (bil [biu̯], dal [dau̯], volk [ʋou̯k], pol [pɔu̯])
word-final obstruents are devoiced before a pause (grad [ɡraːt], gozd [ɡɔːst], mož [moːʃ])
obstruent clusters take the voicing of their last member (glasba [ˈɡlaːzba], sladko [ˈslaːtkɔ]); /ʋ/ neither causes nor undergoes the assimilation
unstressed mid vowels are only open-mid [ɛ ɔ]; the close-mid vowels /e o/ occur only under stress
syllabic r is pronounced [ər] (trg [tərk], smrt [smərt], rdeč [ərˈdɛːt͡ʃ])
lj and nj are [lj], [nj] before a vowel and plain [l], [n] (for some speakers slightly palatalised) before a consonant or word-finally (konj [kɔn], polje [ˈpɔːljɛ])
/n/ is [ŋ] before velars; /x/ is [ɣ] before voiced obstruents; /r/ is a tap or short trill
colloquial Ljubljana speech reduces and drops unstressed /i/ and /u/; the standard does not
phonotactics: close-mid /e o/ and long vowels only in stressed syllables
short stressed vowels mainly in final syllables; stressed schwa is always short
no voiced obstruents before a pause
sonorant plus obstruent onsets are broken by schwa or a syllabic variant (rdeč, lgati)

stress.rule: Stress can fall on any syllable and is not shown in ordinary spelling; dictionaries mark it with accent marks that also show length and vowel quality (á é í ó ú long close, ê ô long open, à è ì ò ù short). A few words have two stresses.
stress.cues: duration (stressed vowels are long apart from the short final type and schwa), intensity, vowel quality (close-mid vowels only under stress) and, in tonemic varieties, pitch

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: the mid vowel contrast is neutralised in unstressed syllables and unstressed vowels are short; standard speech keeps them, colloquial central speech deletes many
rhythm.notes: The class label is an impression from the descriptive literature; no rhythm-metric study is cited.

length.notes: In the traditional norm length is contrastive only under stress. Acoustic studies (Srebot-Rejec 1988; Petek, Šuštaršič & Komar 1996) found little or no duration difference between the traditional long and short stressed vowels in present-day standard speech, so many analyses now treat length as a property of stress. Unstressed vowels are always short.

intonation.declarative: falling: the nuclear stressed syllable is followed by low pitch to the end
intonation.yes_no_question: rise on or after the last stressed syllable; questions introduced by the particle ali (a) can also fall
intonation.wh_question: falling, with a high question word
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: non-tonemic speech: high or falling pitch on the stressed syllable; tonemic speech: the shape depends on the toneme (see tone)
intonation.notes: In tonemic speech the sentence contour is added to the word tonemes; in final position the acute rises less in statements.

inventory.name: acute (low or rising toneme), written á in tonemic notation
inventory.description: the stressed syllable is low or slightly rising and the following syllable is higher; on a final syllable the rise is within the syllable

inventory.name: circumflex (high or falling toneme), written ȃ in tonemic notation
inventory.description: the stressed syllable is high and falling and the following syllable is low

inventory.name: short accent, written ȁ or à in tonemic notation
inventory.description: short stressed vowel, mostly in final syllables; tonal contrast is marginal and the pitch is usually falling like the circumflex

tone.neutral_tone: unstressed syllables carry no toneme: before the stress they are mid, after an acute the first post-tonic syllable is high, after a circumflex it is low
tone.notes: Chao numerals are a schematic rendering of the published descriptions (Šuštaršič, Komar & Petek 1999; Srebot-Rejec 1988; Toporišič 2000), not measured values. The tonemic contrast exists only in part of the standard-speaking community; a synthesiser that uses stress alone (circumflex-like fall on every stressed syllable) produces an accepted standard pronunciation.

problems: Stress is put on the penultimate syllable by default (marked 'Temporary' in tr_languages.c) and the word list has only about 250 entries; Slovenian stress is lexical, so many words are wrong unless the text carries accent marks (slovenščina, otrok, rdeč, rjav).

Every stressed vowel is made long and stressed e, o default to close-mid [eː oː]. Open-mid /ɛː ɔː/ and stressed schwa cannot be seen in the spelling and are mostly missed: voda, gora, noga get [oː] instead of [ɔː]; pes, dež get [eː] instead of [ə]; short final stressed vowels are lengthened (brat, kmet).
No pitch accent: acute and circumflex are not distinguished (no tone phonemes in the phoneme table). This matches the non-tonemic standard only.
Word-final nj is the palatal nasal [ɲ] (konj); the standard has [n].
Only the default eSpeak tunes are used; wh-questions get the same fall-rise as yes-no questions.
good: accent marks in the text select stress, length and open or close quality (vôda [ˈʋɔːda], otròk [ɔˈtrɔk], máti)
final devoicing and regressive voicing assimilation (grad, gozd, glasba, sladko, predsednik)
l and v as [w] or [u] in the right positions (volk, bil, dal, vzeti, vsak)
schwa with syllabic r (trg [tərk], smrt, vrt)
unstressed e, o are open-mid; v is the approximant [ʋ]

notes: No formant, VOT or rhythm-metric values are given because I cannot quote published figures with confidence; Petek, Šuštaršič & Komar (1996) report formant measurements for the standard vowels.
